analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-based public health plan on the insurance exchanges and expands premium subsidies.
analysis.headline: A bill to create a public Medicare-style health plan and lift the cap on premium subsidies was introduced December 4, 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has seen no further action; it has 10 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have the federal government offer its own health plan, built on Medicare, for sale on the same marketplaces where people buy individual and small-employer coverage starting in 2028. It would pay doctors and hospitals Medicare rates (up to 50% higher in rural areas), require providers who take Medicare or Medicaid to accept the plan, and let the Health Secretary negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers. It also lifts the income cap on premium tax credits, fixes the 'family glitch,' and spends $30 billion over three years pooling the costs of the sickest patients to bring premiums down for everyone.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy coverage on their own or through a small employer, especially households above 400% of the poverty line who today lose all premium help, and families locked out of subsidies by the family-glitch rule. The plan's free primary care and Medicare-level payment rates would put price pressure on private insurers and hospitals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People buying individual or small-group coverage

how_it_helps.text: Creates a public 'Medicare Exchange health plan' available in every rating area of the individual and small-group markets starting plan year 2028, offered at silver and gold levels with no cost-sharing for primary care.
Removes the 400%-of-poverty income cap on premium tax credits, so higher-earning households no longer lose subsidies all at once, and caps their premium contribution at 8.5% of income.
Fixes the 'family glitch,' allowing family members to get subsidies when employer coverage is unaffordable for them even if it is affordable for the employee.
Pays providers under the plan at Medicare rates, with authority to raise rates up to 50% in rural areas, which the plan can use to offer cheaper premiums than private insurers.

Establishes a national reinsurance program, authorized at $10 billion for each of fiscal years 2028 through 2030, to pool the costs of the highest-cost patients and reduce premiums for all individual coverage on and off the exchanges.

Gives the Health Secretary authority to negotiate prescription drug prices by striking the Medicare Part D provision that bars the Secretary from intervening in price negotiations between manufacturers and plans.

Appropriates $1 billion each to a plan reserve fund and a data and technology fund for fiscal year 2027 to stand up the plan, and authorizes $50 million for the Justice Department's Antitrust Division and $100 million for the FTC to study and police anticompetitive practices in health care markets.
Bars providers that restrict or exclude patients on the public plan from federal health programs unless they exempt or equally treat plan enrollees.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the startup funds, the $30 billion reinsurance program, and the larger subsidy pool. Hospitals and physicians accept Medicare-level payment rates and must participate in the plan to keep their Medicare and Medicaid enrollment. Private insurers gain a government competitor, and brand-name drug makers lose protection from direct price negotiation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, hospitals, doctors, insurers, drug makers

drawbacks.text: Because the public plan pays Medicare rates, which are generally below what commercial insurers pay, some hospitals and physician practices could face lower revenue, and providers may seek the bill's narrow 'exceptional circumstances' opt-out, which could mean thinner networks for patients.

The expanded tax credits, reinsurance authorization, and startup funds cost the federal treasury; the bill does not specify an offset for the additional subsidy spending beyond the plan's requirement that premiums cover its own actuarial cost.

The reinsurance program pools the costs of the sickest patients across the whole individual market, which props up premiums for private insurers as well as the public plan rather than targeting aid only to the public option.
Mandatory participation for Medicare and Medicaid providers, with a limited opt-out, is a real constraint on practices that believe below-market payment rates threaten their ability to operate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households buying coverage on the exchanges — especially those above the subsidy cliff and families hit by the family glitch — the gains are substantial and concrete. The costs are real but mostly diffuse: federal spending on subsidies and reinsurance, and lower payment rates concentrated on hospitals and doctors, who argue this could narrow access. The bill's design leans on Medicare rates to keep the public plan's premiums low, which is the affordability engine but also the main source of provider friction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in early December 2025, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Bennet introduced the Medicare-X Choice Act of 2025 in the Senate on December 4, 2025, joined by Sens. Kaine, Booker, Duckworth, Smith, Warnock, Hickenlooper, and Klobuchar.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced, and the action history shows no further action.
Ten senators, all Democrats, have signed on as cosponsors.
Republicans hold 55 seats in this Senate and none has cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the current system's incumbents: private insurers, hospitals, and brand-name drug makers face no new public competitor, and households above the subsidy cap still pay full premiums.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, hospitals, and drug makers, for now

for.name: Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and described it as establishing a public health plan on the exchanges.

for.name: 10 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all ten cosponsors are Democrats.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since it was referred to his committee in December 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats (10 of 45 Senate Democrats have signed on), no Republican has supported it, and the bill sits with a Republican chair and a 55-47 Republican majority.

industries.note: The public plan would compete directly with private insurers on the exchanges at Medicare-level prices, but the bill also routes all expanded tax credits through exchange coverage and spends $30 billion on reinsurance that props up private plans' premiums. Insurers' interest is against the affordability gains the bill offers consumers.

The plan pays Medicare rates, typically below commercial rates, and providers cannot stay enrolled in Medicare or Medicaid without participating in the plan. Their financial interest runs against the plan's low premiums, though rural providers could see rates raised up to 50%.

Striking the Part D non-interference provision gives the Health Secretary authority to negotiate Medicare drug prices directly, and the public plan must pay drug rates the Secretary negotiates. Manufacturers lose the statutory protection that has kept the government out of those negotiations.

analysis.trajectory: Bills like this are routinely referred to committee and rarely get a hearing, let alone a floor vote. With Republicans holding a 55-47 Senate majority, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action since the December 2025 referral, the realistic path is that it stalls in Finance this Congress unless support broadens sharply.
